title: What a degradability landscape can tell us about protein degraders
What a degradability landscape can tell us about protein degraders
text:
The central assessment
Du and colleagues present a framework for organizing the factors that determine protein degradation. Its effective processing constant, kpr, serves much the same mathematical role as the catalytic constant in earlier models. The framework is useful, but the paper does not establish that kpr is a superior predictive or mechanistic parameter.
Targeted protein degradation creates an appealing optimization problem. A compound must bring a target and an E3 ligase together, enable productive ubiquitination, and remove protein faster than the cell replaces it. Binding affinity measures only part of that process. DMAX and DC50 summarize its outcome, but do not directly identify the limiting step.
In A quantitative approach for defining the degradability landscape of protein degraders, Du and colleagues connect these processes in a compact model 1. They calculate ternary-complex abundance, combine it with endogenous protein turnover, and introduce an effective processing constant, Kpr. Varying target affinity and this constant produces a landscape of predicted degradation depth and potency.
What interested me most was whether this framework adds explanatory power beyond the mathematics already available, and whether its validation supports using fitted parameters to guide chemistry.
The paper deserves credit for making a complicated system easier to explore. My concern is the biological meaning assigned to a parameter estimated from the very degradation response it is intended to explain.

title: What a degradability landscape can tell us about protein degraders
section: How much is new in the rate constant?
text:
How much is new in the rate constant?
The authors describe target abundance using a balance between synthesis, natural turnover, and degrader-induced loss:
\[
\frac{dP}{dt}=k_{\mathrm{sp}}-k_{\mathrm{dp}}P-k_{\mathrm{pr}}[PLE].
\]
Here, [PLE] is the modeled target-degrader-E3 complex. The product kpr[PLE] is the induced degradation flux. The constant represents processing per unit of ternary complex, rather than disappearance of the entire target pool.
That distinction is valid. More target can generate more ternary complex and a larger absolute degradation flux without requiring the processing constant to change. The underlying turnover logic, however, is not new; it has been represented in several earlier mathematical and pharmacodynamic models.
Haid and Reichel’s 2023 framework already expressed the same balance using a catalytic constant and ternary target engagement 2. Defining \(p=P/P_0\) and \(TE=[PLE]/P\), Du’s equation becomes:
\[
\frac{dp}{dt}=k_{\mathrm{dp}}(1-p)-k_{\mathrm{pr}}TE\,p.
\]
This is the earlier turnover equation with kpr occupying the role of kcat. Haid and Reichel’s framework also includes binding affinities, cooperativity, E3 abundance, time dependence, the hook effect, and combined inhibition and degradation. Its minimum mechanistic inputs are target and E3 concentrations, target and E3 binding affinities, cooperativity, intracellular degrader concentration, target half-life, simulation time, and a catalytic degradation constant. The same system can also be represented empirically from time-resolved concentration-response data using Dmax, DC50, and endogenous turnover.
Du and colleagues require target and E3 copy number, target half-life, degrader-target KD, degrader-E3 KD, cooperativity, intracellular degrader concentration, simulation time, and a degradation observation from which kpr is fitted.
The implementations have differences. Du and colleagues update equilibrium complex abundance as the target is depleted, while Haid and Reichel developed an unsaturated approximation after presenting the fuller equilibrium expression. Nevertheless, the algebra shows substantial continuity. A new name for the effective constant does not demonstrate a new mechanistic quantity.
My interpretation. The contribution is strongest as an implementation and application: integrating proteomics inputs, calibrating systems with limited degradation data, and presenting an accessible landscape. The approach still requires several difficult-to-measure or assumed inputs. Establishing that it performs better requires a comparison with the earlier framework using matched inputs and withheld observations.

title: What a degradability landscape can tell us about protein degraders
section: What does a fitted processing constant actually contain?
text:
What does a fitted processing constant actually contain?
The paper estimates \(k_{\mathrm{pr}}\) after supplying other parameters, including target half-life, protein abundance, binding affinity, and cooperativity. Some come from public datasets; others are approximated.
My concern is that degradation data constrain the combined action of processing and engagement:
\[
k_{\mathrm{induced}}=k_{\mathrm{pr}}TE.
\]
If modeled engagement is too low, a larger fitted processing constant can compensate. A unique numerical fit therefore need not identify a unique biological mechanism.
For example, in a weak-occupancy regime, ternary-complex abundance is approximately proportional to effective E3 concentration. Underestimating that concentration threefold can inflate the fitted processing constant approximately threefold while preserving the predicted degradation response. Exposure and cooperativity errors can produce similar compensation.
This does not make the parameter useless. It makes its interpretation conditional. A low fitted value might reflect inefficient ubiquitination or proteasomal processing, but it might also reflect incorrect assumptions about intracellular exposure or accessible protein pools. Those explanations imply different medicinal-chemistry decisions.

title: What a degradability landscape can tell us about protein degraders
section: A correlation of 0.95 with conditional reconstruction
text:
A correlation of 0.95 with conditional reconstruction
In the BTK analysis, the authors fixed the measured BTK KD, target and CRBN copy numbers, BTK half-life, degrader-CRBN KD, cooperativity, and a 24-hour simulation window. They then varied kpr until the model’s simulated absolute DC50 matched the experimentally measured DC50, and used that fitted kpr to calculate DMAX.
The required inputs for each compound-cell-line observation were:

Fix the experimentally measured BTK binding \(K_D\).
Fix externally supplied parameters:

BTK copy number: 22,692 molecules/cell
CRBN copy number: 12,265 molecules/cell
BTK half-life: 71.9 h
degrader–CRBN \(K_D\): 3.84 μM
cooperativity: \(\alpha=1\)
simulation time: 24 h

Measured DC50, used to select the closest fitted kpr.

Therefore, the reported r = 0.95 does not represent an independent prediction from biochemical parameters. DC50 and DMAX were generated from the same degradation assay, and DC50 was used to calibrate the model before DMAX was estimated. The analysis is best described as conditional reconstruction. The robustness and transferability of kpr therefore remain open questions.
The rationale rests on a familiar mass-balance principle: changed protein level equals intrinsic synthesis minus intrinsic degradation minus degrader-induced degradation. The authors add PLE, the modeled ternary-complex concentration, which can represent cellular engagement more explicitly. However, PLE requires several inputs, some of which are difficult to measure and others of which are estimated. Those assumptions can reduce the reliability of the inferred kpr.
There is also a consequential definition issue. This paper uses absolute DC50, the concentration producing 50% depletion. The earlier framework uses half-maximal degradation, meaning half of DMAX. For a Hill-one concentration-response curve, algebra gives:
\[
DC_{50,\mathrm{absolute}}=\frac{DC_{50,\mathrm{relative}}}{2D_{\max}-1}.
\]
At 60% DMAX, absolute DC50 is five times relative DC50. Below 50% DMAX, absolute DC50 does not exist. The THP-1 observation with 36% DMAX is consequently absent from the comparison.
This selection is understandable, but it limits the claim: the analysis does not establish that the model distinguishes effective from ineffective degraders. Nor is the DMAX prediction an exact tautology; DMAX was not directly fitted, and the relationship still imposes a constraint.
Within-cell correlations are approximately 0.918 in Ramos and 0.916 in THP-1. Those values are high, but they should not be read as proof of accurate absolute prediction. Removing the low-DMAX Ramos observation reduces the correlation to approximately 0.526 among the remaining six compounds, whose observed DMAX values span only 84-87%.
The defensible criticism is specific: a small, selected dataset shows ordering with substantial calibration error, and performance within a narrow chemical response range is sensitive to an influential observation.

title: How photoproximity labeling uncovered a hidden regulator of c-Myc
text:
iLo

2026-09-04
c-Myc is one of the best-studied cancer proteins, yet it remains difficult to drug directly. One alternative is to identify proteins that cancer cells use to maintain c-Myc expression or stability. The study by Milione and colleagues takes this approach and finds SLK—a kinase that conventional mutation- or expression-centered searches would have been unlikely to prioritize [1].
What interested me most was not simply the addition of another kinase to the c-Myc network. It was why SLK had escaped detection for so long.

title: How photoproximity labeling uncovered a hidden regulator of c-Myc
section: The relevant signal was invisible to conventional databases
text:
The relevant signal was invisible to conventional databases
SLK would not stand out as an obvious cancer driver in a typical bioinformatics analysis. It is not commonly defined by recurrent cancer mutations, strong gene amplification, or a striking increase in bulk RNA or protein abundance. Although SLK and c-Myc show some degree of co-dependency in certain cancer cell lines, co-dependency alone does not reveal the biological connection between them.
The paper suggests that the important variable is neither total SLK expression nor mutation status. It is which SLK isoform is expressed and where that isoform is located.
PC-3 cells preferentially express SLK-L, a longer splice isoform containing exon 13 and a putative nuclear localization signal. Total SLK abundance was similar among the prostate cell lines examined, but nuclear SLK was elevated in PC-3 cells. This brings SLK into the same compartment as c-Myc and creates an opportunity for a functional interaction [1].
This is the type of relationship that conventional cancer databases are poorly equipped to uncover. Gene-level RNA analysis often combines multiple transcripts into one value. Standard proteomics may quantify total SLK without reliably distinguishing SLK-L from SLK-S. Even a dependency screen can tell us only that a cell needs SLK. It cannot explain whether that dependency involves c-Myc, mitosis, focal adhesions, or another SLK function.

My interpretation. The paper supports SLK-L as the likely c-Myc-relevant isoform. It does not establish that only SLK-L can stabilize c-Myc, because the authors did not directly compare the two isoforms in a controlled rescue experiment. SLK-S might also support c-Myc if it were artificially directed into the nucleus. That distinction would show whether exon 13 contributes a unique molecular function or mainly provides nuclear access.

The broader conclusion is persuasive: a cancer dependency can arise from altered splicing and localization without producing a conspicuous change in total RNA or protein. A database search centered on mutation and expression would probably never have prioritized SLK as a c-Myc regulator.

title: How photoproximity labeling uncovered a hidden regulator of c-Myc
section: A short snapshot of the c-Myc neighborhood
text:
A short snapshot of the c-Myc neighborhood
The authors found SLK using µMap, a photoproximity-labeling method. They attached an iridium photocatalyst to c-Myc in biochemically intact isolated nuclei, added a diazirine-biotin probe, and irradiated the sample with blue light for one minute. Light activation generated short-lived reactive carbenes that labeled proteins close to c-Myc—within an estimated radius of approximately 4 nm in this implementation [1,2].
This short labeling period is important. Methods such as BioID use a promiscuous biotin ligase and typically integrate proximity over much longer labeling windows [3]. That broad history can be useful, but it also creates a larger candidate list when the bait is a mobile nuclear protein associated with extensive chromatin complexes.
In a same-cell-line comparison in PC-3 cells, BioID yielded 1,563 proteins and µMap yielded 519. Both methods recovered comparable numbers of known c-Myc interactions, but SLK was enriched by µMap and not identified by BioID [1]. The smaller µMap result reduced the candidate space by roughly threefold.
The comparison does not prove that spatial resolution alone explains the difference. The experiments also differed in labeling duration, cellular compartment, fusion design, reaction chemistry, acquisition method, and proteasome-inhibitor treatment. BioID was performed in whole cells over 24 hours, whereas µMap captured a one-minute interval in isolated nuclei [1].
For me, the value of µMap is therefore not simply that it labels a smaller radius. Its more useful feature is experimental control. The investigator can choose the compartment and the moment in which the protein neighborhood is recorded. This may help uncover low-abundance or conditional interactions that disappear inside a large, time-integrated interactome.

title: How photoproximity labeling uncovered a hidden regulator of c-Myc
section: How strongly does SLK regulate c-Myc?
text:
How strongly does SLK regulate c-Myc?
The functional data go well beyond the initial proximity signal. SLK co-immunoprecipitated with c-Myc in PC-3 cells. Knocking out SLK reduced c-Myc protein to approximately 20% of the wild-type level, while the reduction in MYC RNA was much smaller [1].
The c-Myc half-life decreased from 138 minutes to 60 minutes after SLK knockout. Under a first-order degradation model, the degradation-rate ratio is:
\[
\frac{k_{\mathrm{KO}}}{k_{\mathrm{WT}}}
= \frac{\ln 2 / 60}{\ln 2 / 138}
= \frac{138}{60}
\approx 2.3
\]
This derived estimate corresponds to an approximately 2.3-fold increase in the apparent degradation rate. Re-expressing c-Myc rescued target-gene expression, proliferation, cell-cycle progression, and cellular morphology after SLK loss. SLK-knockout cells also failed to establish tumors in the reported PC-3 xenograft experiment [1].
Together, these experiments make a strong case that SLK supports c-Myc stability and c-Myc-dependent growth in PC-3 cells.

title: How photoproximity labeling uncovered a hidden regulator of c-Myc
section: The proposed mechanism is not yet closed
text:
The proposed mechanism is not yet closed
The authors propose that SLK phosphorylates c-Myc at serine 329, which reduces GSK3β-dependent phosphorylation at threonine 58 and protects c-Myc from degradation. Recombinant SLK phosphorylated c-Myc at S329 in vitro; an S329A c-Myc mutant was less stable, whereas the phosphomimetic S329D mutant was more stable. In vitro experiments and a cellular proximity-ligation assay also support competition between SLK and GSK3β for c-Myc binding [1].
However, the paper does not demonstrate that endogenous S329 phosphorylation falls after SLK knockout. It also does not show that wild-type SLK rescues c-Myc stability while kinase-dead SLK fails to do so. SLK may phosphorylate c-Myc directly in cells, but it could also stabilize c-Myc partly by acting as a scaffold or by interfering with GSK3β binding.

The experiment I would run next
Compare SLK-L, kinase-dead SLK-L, SLK-S, and nuclear-targeted SLK-S in SLK-knockout PC-3 cells. Measure endogenous c-Myc S329 and T58 phosphorylation together with c-Myc half-life.

If only catalytically active SLK-L rescues the phenotype, kinase activity and isoform context are both required.
If nuclear-targeted SLK-S rescues, exon 13 may act mainly through localization.
If kinase-dead nuclear SLK still provides partial rescue, scaffolding or competition with GSK3β probably contributes.


That comparison would separate catalytic activity from localization and scaffolding.

title: How photoproximity labeling uncovered a hidden regulator of c-Myc
section: Could µMap help identify E3-ligase substrates?
text:
Could µMap help identify E3-ligase substrates?
The study also made me think about a broader application. Photoproximity labeling may be particularly useful for finding substrates of E3 ubiquitin ligases.
E3–substrate interactions are often weak and transient. Once ubiquitinated, the substrate may leave the ligase complex and be degraded rapidly. A long labeling window can accumulate many proteins that share a compartment with the E3 ligase but are not substrates. A short pulse could provide a cleaner snapshot of proteins present near the ligase during substrate recognition.
Compartment control would add another advantage. The same E3 ligase can encounter different substrates in the nucleus, cytoplasm, or at specific membranes. Restricting µMap to one compartment could reduce unrelated proteins and expose context-specific substrates.

Proposed application—not established by this paper. Proximity alone would not show that a labeled protein is an E3 substrate. Useful controls would include a ligase-dead mutant, acute proteasome inhibition, time-resolved labeling, and direct measurements of ubiquitination or protein stability. Comparing active and inactive ligases could distinguish proteins that merely occupy the same space from proteins whose proximity depends on catalytic substrate engagement.

That may be where photoproximity labeling has its greatest value. It does not replace genetics, biochemistry, or ubiquitin proteomics. It gives those methods a shorter and more biologically focused list of candidates to test.

title: How photoproximity labeling uncovered a hidden regulator of c-Myc
text:
What would change my mind?
My interpretation would weaken if controlled isoform-rescue experiments showed that SLK-S supports c-Myc stability without nuclear localization, if loss of SLK left endogenous c-Myc S329 phosphorylation unchanged under conditions with verified assay sensitivity, or if the SLK–c-Myc dependency failed to reproduce beyond the reported cellular contexts.
The current study nevertheless illustrates a useful principle. SLK was not hidden because nobody had measured its RNA or protein. It was hidden because the relevant biology depended on an isoform entering the right compartment and approaching c-Myc during a limited interaction window. µMap provided a way to see that event.

Evidence note
Reported: interactome sizes, localization, co-immunoprecipitation, knockout effects, half-lives, rescue experiments, xenograft outcome, and the biochemical S329/GSK3β experiments come from Milione and colleagues [1].
Derived: the approximately 2.3-fold change in apparent degradation rate is calculated above from the reported half-lives, assuming first-order degradation.
Inferred: SLK-L is probably the c-Myc-relevant isoform, but isoform specificity and the necessity of SLK catalytic activity remain incompletely tested.
Proposed: the E3-ligase application and the four-arm SLK rescue experiment are the author’s suggestions.
